Cross-Sectional Equity Alpha: From Data Inspection to Backtest

A rigorous, point-in-time research study

Author

Ying Sun

Published

June 2, 2026

Abstract

We build a tradable, dollar-neutral cross-sectional equity alpha from a panel of anonymised security reference data, proprietary signals (d1–d11) and risk factors (rf1–rf6) spanning 2010–2017. The study runs end-to-end: data inspection and quality control, point-in-time feature and target construction, model selection on the information coefficient (IC), and a walk-forward out-of-sample backtest. Every step is constructed to be free of look-ahead bias; we are explicit about where rigour matters and quantify the cost of getting it wrong. The final book is an ensemble forecast traded as a risk-factor-neutral, dollar-neutral portfolio.

1 Introduction

1.1 Objective

The goal is to turn raw, anonymised cross-sectional data into a tradable equity alpha and to evaluate it honestly. Concretely, for each security \(i\) and trading day \(t\) we forecast a forward return, rank securities cross-sectionally, and hold a dollar-neutral book (long notional = short notional) rebalanced under realistic trading costs. Success is measured by the net (after-cost) Sharpe ratio of the walk-forward out-of-sample equity curve, supported by the forecast’s information coefficient (IC).

Two principles guide the whole study:

  1. No look-ahead. Every transform that touches a date \(t\) uses information available at or before \(t\) only — cross-sectional normalisation is computed within a single day, the target is a strictly forward return, and models are trained on trailing windows.
  2. Honest evaluation. Where a modelling choice can silently leak information (feature selection, hyper-parameter tuning, normalisation statistics), we isolate it and report the out-of-sample consequence rather than an in-sample flatter.

1.2 Data

The project provides three families of files over 2010–2017 (≈8.8M security-day rows, ~2,000 tradable names per day):

Family Contents
Security reference data_date, security_id, close_price, volume, group_id (industry), in_trading_universe, ret1d (daily return)
Signals d1–d11, one proprietary signal per file, keyed by (data_date, security_id)
Risk factors rf1–rf6, exposures used for neutralisation

Only names with in_trading_universe == "Y" are holdable; the realised daily return ret1d is the raw material for the forecast target.

1.3 Pipeline overview

The work is organised as three notebooks, mirrored by the sections of this report:

  1. data_inspection.ipynb — schema, data-quality audit, signal diagnostics (Section 2 below).
  2. alpha_model.ipynb — feature/target engineering, IC-based model selection, and the honest walk-forward forecast.
  3. portfolio_construction.ipynb — alpha → dollar-neutral weights, the backtest engine, risk-factor neutralisation, and performance reporting.

1.4 Summary of results

The final model is an ensemble (an IC-weighted signal composite blended with a regularised linear model) traded as a risk-factor-neutral, dollar-neutral book, rebalanced weekly net of 1 bp. Over the full walk-forward out-of-sample window (2011–2017) it achieves a net Sharpe of ≈1.4 at ~3.4% annualised volatility. Crucially, this number is reported against an honest baseline: removing the look-ahead present in a naïve setup takes a headline Sharpe of ~0.74 down to ~0.40 before our improvements rebuild it on solid ground. The rigour story — what leaked, what we removed, and what we tested and rejected — is developed in the modelling and results sections.

2.3 Returns: distribution and outliers

The daily return ret1d is sharply leptokurtic and contaminated by extreme values: across 8.79M observations the standard deviation (0.38) is dominated by tails, with 482 rows of \(|r|>1\) and a maximum of +1099 (i.e. +109,900%) — clearly data errors rather than tradable moves. There are 8,854 missing returns.

ImportantConsequence for the pipeline

These outliers must be neutralised before they can distort any cumulative or moment-based feature. Downstream we winsorise ret1d cross-sectionally per day before building the target and any return-based statistic, rather than trusting raw values.

2.4 Forward-return target alignment (no look-ahead)

The forecast target is the forward return ret1d_fwd(i,t) = ret1d(i, t+2). The subtlety is that a security can leave the universe and re-enter months later: a naïve shift(-2) would then pair a pre-gap row with a post-gap return and silently fabricate a “forward” return that spans the hole. We therefore compute the shift only within chunks of consecutive trading days (a gap > 5 trading days opens a new chunk), so no return is ever paired across a gap. The output below shows a worked example (security 1031, which exits in 2015-07 and re-enters in 2015-10) and the chunking statistics.

2.6 Duplicate-key audit

Several signal files violate the (data_date, security_id) key. The audit classifies each affected file as exact-copy duplicates (safe to drop) versus conflicting values (genuinely multi-valued and must be aggregated).

ImportantResolution
  • d3, d4 — 127,266 duplicate-key pairs that are exact copies (0 conflicting) → de-duplicate by dropping.
  • d9 — ~8.0M duplicate-key pairs, of which 4.3M conflict (median relative difference ~1%) → genuinely multi-valued per key, so we collapse it into two features: the per-key mean (d9_mean) and spread (d9_spread).

2.7 Signal coverage and forecasting power

The headline diagnostic table reports, per signal: coverage (fraction of tradable name-days observed), the daily cross-sectional IC, its annualised information ratio, and hit rate. This is what tells us which signals carry tradable information before any model is fit.

A signal is only useful if its IC is persistent, not concentrated in one regime; we therefore inspect the rolling IC through time.

NoteKey finding

A handful of signals carry most of the cross-sectional information (the strongest by |IC| are d3, d1, d6 (negative), d5 and d2); several others are weak. The sign and strength are learned per training window downstream, but this diagnostic explains why a sparse, robust combination later beats a kitchen-sink regression.

2.9 Collinearity and a redundant signal

Some signal pairs are strongly related; one pair is perfectly redundant.

ImportantResolution

d10 and d11 are identical (rank correlation 1.0) → d11 is dropped to avoid double-counting. The Pearson-vs-Spearman comparison also shows several pairs that look uncorrelated under raw Pearson but are strongly monotone — heavy tails wreck linear correlation — reinforcing the choice of rank-based methods downstream.

2.10 Risk factors

Finally we characterise the six risk factors and confirm the signals are not merely disguised factor exposures — a precondition for the risk-factor neutralisation that later drives the Sharpe.

risk factor frame: (8800015, 8) | factors: ['rf1', 'rf2', 'rf3', 'rf4', 'rf5', 'rf6']
date range: 20100104 to 20171229

pct missing per factor:
rf1   0
rf2   0

rf5   0
rf6   0
dtype: float64
NoteKey finding

No signal is strongly correlated with any risk factor, so the alpha is largely orthogonal to the factor structure. This is what makes risk-factor neutralisation (Section 6) a near-free volatility reduction rather than a destruction of signal.

TipData-inspection takeaways carried forward
  1. Winsorise ret1d per day before any return-based feature (outliers up to +1099).
  2. Build the forward target with chunk-aware shifting (no cross-gap leakage).
  3. De-duplicate d3/d4; collapse d9 into mean + spread; drop the redundant d11.
  4. Use rank-based normalisation (heavy tails, mixed sign, monotone-but-non-linear).
  5. Signals are ~orthogonal to risk factors → neutralisation is cheap insurance.
